content: These options include combinations such as metformin with DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT-2 inhibitors, or thiazolidinediones (TZDs); sulfonylurea with DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT-2 inhibitors, or TZDs; or triple therapy involving metformin, sulfonylurea, and one of the aforementioned agents. Insulin therapy may also be introduced, either alone or in combination with oral agents, depending on the patient’s clinical needs. For individuals with type 1 diabetes, the outcomes of treatment with short-acting analogue insulins are compared to those with short-acting human insulins. Similarly, the outcomes of long-acting analogue insulins are compared to intermediate-acting human insulins. These comparisons assess critical outcomes such as glycemic control, severe hypoglycemia, cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality, and quality of life. In type 2 diabetes, the effectiveness of short-acting analogue insulins is also compared to short-acting human insulins, and long-acting analogue insulins are compared to intermediate-acting human insulins. The evaluation focuses on critical outcomes like HbA1c levels, body weight, severe hypoglycemia, and cost-effectiveness. Critical outcomes for type 2 diabetes include glycemic control (HbA1c), CVD mortality and incidence, severe hypoglycemia, body weight, quality of life, and cost-effectiveness. Important outcomes include all-cause mortality, mild hypoglycemia, progression of nephropathy, visual impairment, and other complications such as infections and fractures. For type 1 diabetes, critical outcomes are similar, with additional emphasis on ketoacidosis and lower limb amputation. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are used to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of various diabetes treatments. For example, sulfonylureas are often compared to newer agents like DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT-2 inhibitors, and TZDs. While industry-funded studies frequently find newer agents to be cost-effective, independent studies often conclude that older, less expensive treatments like sulfonylureas remain more cost-effective in many settings. Patient preferences and treatment satisfaction are also important considerations in diabetes management. Studies show that while newer oral hypoglycemic agents (OHAs) and insulin therapies offer additional options, their higher costs may limit accessibility. Balancing clinical goals with patient preferences and well-being is essential in selecting the most appropriate treatment strategy.
